news.title: Lone juror’s holdout in the Lindsay Clancy trial is a true act of courage
news.text:
‘He couldn’t get over the fact that Clancy viciously killed her children.”

Those are the words of one of the insufferably condescending female jurors from the Lindsay Clancy mistrial who have gone public with their disdain for the lone male juror who refused to go along with their not guilty verdict.

Good for him.

The children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, have been the forgotten victims in this case.

The Massachusetts nurse does not dispute that she strangled her children one by one on Jan. 24, 2023, with exercise bands around their necks after she sent her husband, Patrick, out on an errand.

Patrick returned to his kids dead and his wife bleeding on the snow-covered yard after she cut her wrists and throat and leaped out a bedroom window 12 feet above the ground, rendering herself paralyzed from the waist down. Rather than accepting blame, Lindsay, 36, pleaded not guilty, claiming she could not tell right from wrong at the time because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, even though evidence for that was thin.

Withstood pressure

A mistrial was called last Friday because the jury of nine women and three men could not agree on a verdict after more than seven days of deliberations so contentious that yelling reportedly could be heard outside the room.

Now that several of the jurors have come out and exposed themselves, we can see the immense pressure that the lone holdout juror was under day after day in that jury room, being harangued and browbeaten by women infuriated that he refused to be persuaded by their self-proclaimed superior wisdom.

Jury forewoman Roni Carlson, a former elementary school teacher, Kellie Farina, a chef for a senior center, and Paula Devlin, who does work for a defense contractor, were interviewed on camera by NBC10 Boston, and it’s hard to imagine a more smug group lacking in self-awareness or any humility. They revealed that there were a number of nurses and teachers on the jury.

“He was very arrogant,” Devlin said of the holdout. “He did not take anything that anybody said.”

She complained there were multiple nurses on the jury who took it on themselves to explain the toxicology reports to the holdout juror.

“He tried to ask a question about the medications,” said Devlin. “We had the toxicology report. We could see exactly the amounts. The nurses in the room spoke to that. And talked to that.

“And they spoke to that . . . And he just completely disregarded the information that they gave him.” As was his right.

Carlson, the forewoman, said she thought they’d won the argument at one point. “He admitted he had reasonable doubt and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited . . . And then he said, ‘But I’m still not going to say that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity.’ ”

As was his right.

Another woman, Juror No. 5, spoke to CBS Boston anonymously in defense of the holdout:

“The majority of people . . . was very firm in their stance and their beliefs from the beginning . . . The standalone juror was not the only one who refused to see things from the other side so I’m going to defend [him]. There were some big personalities in that room.”

Originally, she thought Lindsay” was guilty and she was criminally responsible for it, and maybe I still believe that in a certain way.” Several other jurors reportedly felt the same way but over time were persuaded to find Lindsay not guilty — all but the holdout.

Lawyer’s big show

The outspoken female jurors absolutely loved Lindsay’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, and gushed about how “entertaining” and “compassionate” he was. In their minds he had proved that Lindsay was not a bad mother and she “loved her children” and that was all that mattered.

Yet Reddington behaved like an emotional bully, inside and outside the court, especially when he put a target on the holdout juror, whom he blamed for the mistrial in an extended public tantrum outside the court on Friday.

“I hope that guy can sleep well at night,” Reddington said. In court he called the same juror a “liar” and said he “stole seven weeks of the life” of the other jurors,” which is rich considering that in the entire seven-week trial Reddington barely mentioned the three entire lives stolen from the Clancy children by his client.

Reddington also fueled false internet rumors that Patrick was involved in the killing of his own children by refusing to exonerate him when asked and instead praising the TikTok sleuths who have damned Patrick.

“I certainly don’t dismiss them. It’s amazing what people on TikTok . . . how they’re able to ferret out facts and they do investigations.”

Reddington must have realized he went too far because this week he appeared on “CBS Mornings” and recanted, saying, “It’s obvious that Patrick was a man who stood by his wife through all of the difficulty. [He] ought to be able to move on with his life.”

Despite Reddington’s flaws, the outspoken female jurors preferred him to prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham, whom they criticized as lacking “compassion” and being “unprofessional.”

For the children

The prosecutors were entirely professional. Did Carlson and pals disdain them because of their plump appearance, because they don’t have time to go to Pilates every morning?

Sprague and Buckingham have 50 years of prosecutorial experience between them and children of their own, earning modest salaries for draining work in child protection cases. They did their best, although their speedy four-day jury selection leaves something to be desired.

Their boss, District Attorney Tim Cruz, who has been protecting the 500,000 residents of Plymouth County for the past 25 years, was heckled relentlessly outside the court Friday.

The son of a plumber with children and grandchildren of his own, he is the longest serving DA in Massachusetts, even though he is a Republican in a Democrat-majority area.

Plymouth has street signs declaring it “America’s Hometown,” since it is where the Pilgrims arrived on the Mayflower in 1620 and founded the first permanent European settlement in New England. The affluent, predominantly white town, which voted for Kamala Harris over Donald Trump by almost 10 points in 2024, also adopted the slogan “No Place for Hate.”

Officials abandoned that name last year, but it still appears on some signs around town.

In spite of the heckling, Cruz spoke with understated dignity, saying: “I understand that this has been an emotional trial for everybody . . . But in the end I bring it all back to the child victims in this case, Cora, Dawson, and Callan . . .

“Children were murdered, and it’s our job to seek justice.”

Justice is important, regardless of feelings. The trial was not just about Lindsay and her tragedy. It was about the children and precedents set for child murder. Already there are reports of at least one copycat murder.

For the sake of all the other children yet to be born, we cannot afford to become a society that normalizes mothers killing their babies.
news.summary: The children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, have been the forgotten victims in this case.
news.author: Miranda Devine

news.title: Trump says activity seen at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, urges Tehran ‘not to get cute’
news.text:
DALLAS: President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the United States may hit Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, urging Tehran to be cautious.

“We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not ‌to get ‌cute because we ‌will have to hit them very hard,” Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention.

Pickaxe Mountain, located near Iran’s heavily damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility, ‌is ‌a fortified site that hosts ‌two deeply buried tunnel complexes.

Trump ‌has been threatening strikes on Pickaxe Mountain since at least mid-July.

The rise in ‌oil and gas prices due to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which began in February, has become a major issue for Trump and his Republican Party in the lead-up to the midterm U.S. elections in November.
news.summary: President Donald Trump warned Iran about potential U.S. action on Pickaxe Mountain. This site is near Iran’s Natanz facility and is observed for suspicious activities.

news.title: Trump says oil prices that spiked because of Iran war likely won’t come down until after midterms
news.text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after US midterm elections.

Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3%, pushing international Brent crude past the $100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the US and Iran escalated.

“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”

The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.

Trump, in an exchange with reporters before traveling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the US

“They’re desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon,” Trump said. He added, “I think the war’s going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer.”

Trump also spoke at length about the war in Iran during his keynote address to the convention Wednesday evening. He acknowledged it caused energy prices to spike and financial markets to struggle, but said it was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Trump also polled the audience, asking, “Does anyone here think Iran should have a nuclear weapon?” The crowd responded with a resounding “no.”

The president at the outset of the war said it would last a matter of weeks. The conflict is now in its seventh month. The US-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20% of the world’s petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.

Trump last week downplayed the conflict as “small potatoes” even as Republicans expressed concern the war will loom large with voters left navigating elevated gas prices and higher inflation.

The US has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

Trump’s prediction that the war won’t be wrapped up until after Nov. 3 comes after Vice President JD Vance last week steered clear of predicting that the conflict would be over by the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trying to hang on to their narrow majorities in Congress.

Vance told reporters he didn’t want to set “artificial timelines” for the war’s end.

“But when you ask, ‘When will this end?’ You’re asking me a question like, ‘When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?’” Vance said. “I think the reality is, I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”

US benchmark crude on Wednesday stood at around $96 a barrel, and US gasoline prices rose sharply overnight.

The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline ticked up 7 cents overnight t o hit $4.22, now more than a dollar above what it cost at this point last year, according to AAA.

Diesel prices, which can have an outsize impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high Friday and have continued to climb since. The average price per gallon rose to $5.94 overnight, up 9 cents from Friday.

Jet fuel has become so expensive that US and international carriers have cut flights while raising fares and fees.

The latest market gyrations come after the US military reported striking five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship and after attacks by an Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group ignited fires at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.
news.summary: President Donald Trump stated that the spike in oil prices due to the Iran war is expected to continue until after the U.S. midterm elections. Prices surged over 3%, crossing the $100 threshold for Brent crude.

news.title: 'Pointless trade war': Trump’s Canada tariffs draw Senate fire
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 10 (IANS) Five Democratic US senators have accused President Donald Trump of deepening a “pointless trade war” with Canada, warning that new tariffs would raise prices, hurt American businesses and push a key ally towards other trading partners, including China. The criticism came after Trump imposed new restrictions on Canadian products in response to Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion in US exports. The White House said Canada’s measures covered steel, dairy and agricultural equipment. Senators Amy Klobuchar, Chris Coons, Patty Murray, Jeanne Shaheen and Elissa Slotkin on Wednesday (local time) said their states depend heavily on commerce with Canada. “The states we represent rely on Canada as a key trading partner and our primary export market,” the senators said in a joint statement. “We have deep ties with our neighbours to the north, and we share one of the world’s most enduring defence partnerships. We have built two powerful nations over many decades by working together, growing our economies together and securing our homelands together.” The senators said the tariffs would affect small businesses, farmers, manufacturers and consumers. “Instead of working with our neighbours, President Trump is doubling down on a pointless trade war with Canada,” they said. “His tariffs will squeeze our states’ small businesses harder and drive costs up for working families. They will raise the cost of the lumber, plywood and construction equipment we need to build new housing.” The lawmakers also said the measures would hurt workers and businesses manufacturing automobiles, aircraft and machinery. They warned that consumers could pay more for milk, clothing and paper products. They claimed Trump’s tariffs had already cost American families as much as $5,000 in some states. The statement did not provide the methodology behind that estimate. The senators also warned that continued trade friction could weaken the United States’ commercial relationships. “While American families and businesses suffer from Trump’s trade wars, partners around the world, including Canada, are increasingly looking to diversify away from the United States and deepen trade ties with other countries including China,” they said. The White House said Trump signed five proclamations under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. The administration said the measures were a response to Canada’s “additional retaliation and continued discriminatory treatment of crucial American exports.” The actions ban certain Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy goods and other products already covered by 50 per cent tariffs. The import bans will take effect on September 29. The administration also removed products including rock salt and cement from the tariffs while adding other goods, ranging from all-terrain vehicles to additional dairy products. Those changes will take effect on September 15. The White House said the measures would apply even to covered goods originating under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. It argued that the action was needed to protect American farmers, manufacturers and workers. Canada and the United States have one of the world’s largest bilateral trading relationships. Klobuchar is a lead sponsor of legislation seeking to revoke the newest global tariffs and the 50 per cent tariffs on Canada. She has also introduced the Trade Review Act with Republican Senator Chuck Grassley and Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell, which would require congressional approval of new tariffs within 60 days.
news.author: Daklu IANS

news.title: Trump invokes dad of wealthy Princess Di boyfriend to make crass joke about Iranians
news.text:
Donald Trump made an off-color reference to the father of Princess Diana’s boyfriend Dodi Al-Fayed during his remarks Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas as he joked about his war in Iran.

The president delivered the keynote address on night one of the two-day convention in Texas, where Republicans are trying to rally support for flagging candidates nationwide in the face of a resurgent Democratic opposition. As he spoke about the war in Iran, he made an unexplained reference to Mohamed Al-Fayed, and mocked his Arabic name in the process.

Speaking about a potential attack on Pickaxe Mountain, an alleged Iranian nuclear site, Trump told a whooping crowd that the U.S. Space Force could “see everything” taking place at secure Iranian facilities: “We can see everything. We can the see tag on their coat. ‘Mohamed Al-Fayed.’

This is a breaking news report. More to follow...
news.summary: Trump makes racist remark about Arab-sounding names as he jokes about his Iran war in Dallas

news.title: Rubio defends US strikes on boats, warns of drug cartel ‘cancer’
news.text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended controversial strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats during a visit to Ecuador on Wednesday, arguing Latin American cartels would “eat these countries alive” if left unchecked.
Hailing a new generation of conservative leaders emerging across the region who are allied with President Donald Trump, Rubio said Washington was finding partners willing to be “very aggressive” against criminal groups.
Since Trump returned to power, the United States has embraced air strikes against vessels plying known trafficking routes in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
According to Pentagon figures, the operations have killed more than 200 people.
Rights groups, fishermen and their relatives have questioned the campaign, alleging vessels were targeted without sufficient evidence of links to trafficking.
Experts have also questioned whether they do anything to curb the flow of cocaine and other drugs to the United States – the world’s largest consumer.

Speaking after talks with President Daniel Noboa in Quito, Rubio said the operations would continue.
“If you don’t confront these groups, they will eat these countries alive,” he warned. “It’s like a cancer that continues to grow until you don’t literally have a state any more.”
“I’m glad that we have leaders in this region that are serious about going after these groups, because if we didn’t, we would have failed country after failed country.”
In recent weeks there have been signs of a shift in tactics, with joint US-Ecuador patrols removing crews from at least six boats before sinking the vessels.
Rubio said decisions were made case by case and depended on the threat posed by a vessel, its location and local laws.
“When you’re conducting a joint operation in territorial waters, you have to reach an understanding as to how those operations are going to occur,” he said.

Asked whether vessels would continue to be destroyed, Rubio replied: “Well again, it depends, and we still blow up ships”.
Later Wednesday, the US military’s Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said American forces executed a “lethal kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean”.
The operation “killed three narco-terrorists,” SOUTHCOM posted on X along with black-and-white footage of a ship exploding in the water and bursting into flames.
In Ecuador alone, more than 25,000 people have been murdered in the last three years as drug gangs have vied for control of trafficking routes.
“We are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” Rubio said.
While in Quito, he announced the designation of one gang, Los Tiguerones, as a “terrorist organisation” and sanctions against seven Ecuadorian former officials.

The Tiguerones made international headlines in early 2024 when masked gang members stormed a TV studio during a live broadcast, firing shots and forcing terrified crew to the ground.
After visiting Colombia and Ecuador, Rubio late Wednesday landed in Lima, where he will meet Peruvian leaders on the last stop of a tour to shore up right-wing allies and bolster US influence across the region.
In Colombia, Rubio pledged to restore “natural relations” with Bogota after years of leftist rule.
He had less warm words for leftist-led Mexico, which he said was stepping up the cartel fight “but it is still not nearly enough”.
“There are territories, vast territories in Mexico that are not governed by the state,” he said. “That threat will have to be confronted one way or the other.”
His last stop is in Peru, which has been led since July by conservative President Keiko Fujimori.
There, he is expected to advance the “Shield of the Americas” initiative, a US-backed security partnership.

news.title: US birthright citizenship debate puts visa families in focus
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 10 (IANS) The citizenship rights of US-born children of temporary visa holders came under renewed scrutiny as Republican lawmakers advocated restrictions and Democrats said the 14th Amendment guaranteed citizenship at birth. During a House Judiciary subcommittee hearing on birthright citizenship, Republicans urged Congress to act after the Supreme Court overturned President Donald Trump’s executive order. Democrats argued that the court had settled the constitutional question. Republican subcommittee chairman Chip Roy said Congress should define the phrase “subject to the jurisdiction thereof” in the amendment. “It is up to Congress to define, subject to the jurisdiction thereof, to put a stop to birth tourism and to uphold the integrity of what it means to be an American citizen,” Roy said. Arguing that the amendment was not intended to grant automatic citizenship to children born to undocumented immigrants or temporary visitors, Roy said the Supreme Court had wrongly relied on its 1898 Wong Kim Ark decision. That case involved the US-born child of immigrants who were legally and permanently domiciled in the country, Roy said. Rosemary Jenks, co-founder and policy director of the Immigration Accountability Project, told the panel that the ruling did not prevent lawmakers from acting. “The Supreme Court’s decision in Barbara overturned an executive order. It did not strip Congress of its constitutional plenary power over immigration and naturalisation,” Jenks said. She urged Congress to amend the Immigration and Nationality Act to establish exceptions for children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary residents. Jenks proposed rules affecting non-immigrant visa holders seeking welfare benefits on behalf of their US-born children. She said such parents should be required to designate a US citizen or lawful permanent resident to receive the benefits for the child. “American citizenship is a precious commodity,” Jenks said. “Our government must zealously protect US citizenship and ensure it is only granted to aliens we have legally invited to permanently join our American community.” Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach asserted that Congress retained the authority to act. He said the Supreme Court had ruled against a broad executive order but had not declared every possible statute on the question unconstitutional. Kobach said a narrower law dealing with birth tourism could produce a different result before the court. Democrats strongly disputed those arguments. Representative Mary Gay Scanlon, the subcommittee’s ranking Democrat, said children born in the United States to undocumented immigrants and visa holders were protected by the amendment. “The American children of undocumented immigrants and the American children of visa holders are persons born here in America,” Scanlon said. She said they were subject to US law from birth and had “an undeniable constitutional claim to the rights, duties and protections of that reciprocal relationship.”

news.title: Trump Defends Republican Leader Booed at RNC Midterm Convention
news.text: President Donald Trump defended Senate Majority Leader John Thune after attendees at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas booed the South Dakota Republican when Trump mentioned his name during his remarks Wednesday night. Video from the event showed the crowd reacting negatively as Trump referenced Thune. Newsweek National Political Correspondent Alex Rouhandeh, who is in attendance, highlighted that at the mention of Thune’s name, the convention hall erupted in boos, reverberating across the various state delegations. The boos were so loud, it was hard to tell whether Thune’s native South Dakota had cheered for him. Eventually, following Trump’s defense, the booing died down. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during midterm elections. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the House and Senate. Amid the wave of boos, Trump said, "No, no, John is working hard. He's got great opposition... from the Democrat Schumer and these guys, they're terrible. He's got great opposition; he's working very hard. He's going to have great success; you watch." "By the way, we've got great Republican Senators," Trump later added. Newsweek reached out to Thune's office via email on Wednesday night for additional information. What To Know Trump has at times publicly pressured Thune over his handling of the Senate, particularly over the president's push for the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and identification at the ballot box. Trump earlier this summer urged Thune to keep the Senate in session until Republicans can pass the legislation, while Thune has said Republicans do not currently have enough votes to advance it. The reaction from the convention crowd highlights the pressure Thune faces from Trump's most loyal supporters as he attempts to lead the Senate Republican Conference. Thune has generally worked with the White House on Trump's agenda, but his approach to the Senate has occasionally put him at odds with members of the party's conservative wing. The episode also underscores Trump's central role at the first-ever Republican midterm convention, where the president has sought to make the 2026 elections a referendum on his administration despite not appearing on the ballot. The two-day Dallas event has been heavily focused on Trump as the GOP works to energize its base ahead of November's midterm elections. This is a developing story that will be updated with additional information. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: The two-day Dallas event has heavily focused on Trump as the GOP works to energize its base ahead of November's midterm elections.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: Trump suggests Strait of Hormuz be renamed Trump Strait
news.text:
DALLAS /Texas/, September 10. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has suggested the Strait of Hormuz be renamed after him.

"I think we should call the Hormuz Strait, we should call it the Trump [Strait]. I should get something out of there. The Trump Strait. It's going to be called, ladies and gentlemen. I'll have an announcement," he told the Republican midterm convention in Texas.

He also said that he is convinced that oil prices would go down after the United States wins the war with Iran. He once again claimed that the United States controls the Strait of Hormuz, which is a major route for oil transit to global markets.
news.summary: The US president separately said he is convinced that oil prices would go down after the US wins the war with Iran
news.author: Tass

news.title: ‘Trump dividend’ or bribery? President promises to pay $5,000 to every US adult — if Republicans win
news.text:
President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that his administration would pay a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” to each American adult if voters deliver Republicans a win in the 2026 midterms.

“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump said of the plan during his speech at the Republican midterm convention in Texas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.”

This is a breaking news story and will be updated with new information.
news.summary: The president offered few details of the plan but said the money would have to be spent in America

news.title: PM to highlight efforts to end US-Iran war at UNGA
news.text:
Bangladesh assumes presidency as General Assembly formally opens in New York• Trump to speak on opening day; PM Shehbaz’s speech on 25th; Pezeshkian’s attendance ‘not yet confirmed’• Renewal on the cards as tenure of panel monitoring Iran sanctions expires during UNGA session

WASHINGTON: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is due to arrive in New York later this month for the UN General Assembly, where he is expected to highlight Pakistan’s efforts to find a peaceful solution to the ongoing US-Iran war.

PM Shehbaz is slated to address the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 25, where the Gulf conflict is expected to overshadow much of the high-level debate.

The official theme of the 81st session is ‘Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All’, and the UNGA debate is expected to run from Sept 22 to 26, with a final sitting on Sept 28.

However, ongoing fighting between Washington and Tehran is expected to feature prominently in discussions among world leaders, particularly over the security of the Strait of Hormuz, regional stability and the possibility of finding a diplomatic way out of the confrontation.

The participation of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also emerging as a key question ahead of the high-level week.

Iran is listed on the tentative speakers’ schedule as the fifth speaker on Sept 23, the second day of the UNGA debate, but a final decision on whether he will travel to New York or not, has not yet been made.

Iranian officials have indicated that Tehran is still assessing the level of participation and attendance, citing what they describe as “illegal conditions” imposed by Washington on the Iranian delegation’s travel and attendance.

US President Donald Trump is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Sept 22, the opening day of the high-level debate, following Brazil, which traditionally opens the general debate.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is also expected to attend reception hosted by President Trump on the same day.

Israel, the other party to the conflict, is scheduled to speak on Sept 24, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu representing his country.

India, meanwhile, is only sending its foreign minister, who is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Sept 26.

According to diplomatic sources, Pakistan is expected to use the forum of the UN General Assembly to underline its position that the conflict should be resolved through negotiations rather than prolonged military confrontation.

The prime minister is also expected to highlight Islamabad’s contacts with countries involved in efforts to de-escalate the situation.

The Iranian issue is already occupying a prominent place on the UN agenda ahead of the arrival of world leaders.

The Security Council is scheduled to vote on Sept 17 on renewing the mandate of the panel of experts monitoring sanctions on Iran. The panel’s mandate expires on Sept 26, during the General Assembly’s high-level week.

The proposed renewal is expected to produce another confrontation between the United States and its Western allies on one side and Russia and China on the other.

Moscow and Beijing have opposed continuation of the monitoring mechanism, arguing that the Security Council no longer has the authority to pursue the matter in its present form.

The dispute is linked to the restoration of UN sanctions on Iran under the “snapback” mechanism after Britain, France and Germany concluded last year that Tehran was not complying with its obligations under the 2015 nuclear agreement. Iran has rejected allegations that it is seeking nuclear weapons.

The Sept 17 vote will therefore come just days before heads of government begin arriving for the General Assembly and could further sharpen the diplomatic divisions surrounding Iran.

For Pakistan, the situation carries additional urgency because of its geographical proximity to the conflict and its economic and security interests in the Gulf region.

The prime minister will be accompanied by a high-level delegation, including senior members of the government, and is expected to hold a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the General Assembly.

The UN session formally opened on Wednesday, with Bangladesh’s Khalilur Rahman assuming the presidency of the 81st General Assembly. Mr Rahman has placed peace and security, restoration of trust in multilateral institutions and UN reform among the priorities of his presidency.

The session also comes ahead of a major change in the UN hierarchy, as it would be the last for current Secretary General Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on Dec 31, 2026.

Published in Dawn, September 10th, 2026

news.title: ‘Call it Trump Strait’: US prez’s Hormuz pitch as he rallies GOP voters
news.text: US President Donald Trump turned his Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas into a showcase for his trademark political rhetoric on Wednesday, suggesting the Strait of Hormuz should be renamed the “Trump Strait” as he sought to rally voters behind the GOP ahead of the November elections.“I think we should call the Hormuz Strait the Trump Strait. I should get something out of it. The Trump Strait,” Trump told the crowd, referring to the strategically vital waterway amid heightened tensions with Iran.Trump also renewed his pitch for renaming Lake Ontario claiming that the water body should be called “Lake America” and suggesting New Mexico could become “New America”. “Canada very much wants to make a deal. They're dying to make a deal. But it's going to be called Lake America,” he said.The remarks came as Trump used his keynote address to make a broader pitch for Republican candidates and his administration’s record. He urged supporters to treat the upcoming midterms as though he himself were on the ballot, despite not being eligible to seek another presidential term.“If we hand America’s future to the radical-left Democrats, our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet,” Trump said. “Vote Republican and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come.”Trump said there were around 35 key Senate and House races and pledged to campaign across the states involved, promising, “We’re gonna have rallies just like this.”He also highlighted his administration’s tax policies, including “No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, and No Tax on Social Security”, while claiming that the US had attracted more than $20 trillion in foreign investment.“This has been the most successful two years financially and every other way in the history of the presidency,” Trump said.The president also defended Senate Majority Leader John Thune after the Texas crowd booed him, saying, “No, no. John is working hard. He’s got great opposition.”Trump separately praised Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is facing a competitive Senate race, while acknowledging criticism of his appearance and speaking style. “He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said, before adding that Paxton “deserves to be your next senator.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. news.title: Talarico says he 'missed the mark' as he backtracks on controversial woke statements
news.text: In a Fox News exclusive interview, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico came out in favor of banning gender surgery for minors and opposed transgender-identifying men competing in women’s sports. Talarico also backtracked on several of his more controversial claims, including saying there are six genders and that "God is nonbinary." This comes as the Texas Senate race, which is surprisingly close according to recent Fox News polling, enters its final months. The race is considered critical to both parties' chances of securing a Senate majority. Talarico is facing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican who has faced controversies of his own. A Republican loss in Texas would significantly impact President Donald Trump's ability to implement his agenda. Fox News spoke with Talarico at a food drive campaign event in Dallas on Tuesday. Talarico’s event took place as the first-ever GOP midterm convention kicked off just miles away in downtown Dallas. TALARICO CAMPAIGNS WITH SURGEON WHO OPERATED ON TRANSGENDER MINORS: ‘WOLF IN SHEEP’S CLOTHING’ Asked whether he would vote as a U.S. senator in favor of a national ban on gender surgery for minors, Talarico answered, "Absolutely." He said, "I've been consistent on this issue," explaining his opposition to a Texas bill to ban transgender surgeries on minors by saying the measure "was overly broad." "If you go back and check, I voted for a major amendment to limit the bill to banning surgeries for minors," he said. "As a lawmaker, my job is to try to sift through everything the bill does. And sometimes there's stuff in it that's really harmful, and I have no choice but to oppose the bill as a whole." "It's why I try to use amendments, to narrow the focus of the bill so that it does exactly what we intend it to do," he continued. "It's what I tried to do with that piece of legislation, and unfortunately the amendment I supported was unsuccessful." In 2023, as a member of the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico voted against a state bill titled SB 14, which prohibited certain gender surgery, puberty blockers and certain hormone treatments for minors. There were 18 amendments to the bill proposed by Democrats, all of which Talarico voted in favor and all of which ultimately failed. In the same interview, Talarico acknowledged that men in women’s sports is a significant issue in Texas. He said, "I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness." "Every sport has to be safe and fair. As a former public school teacher, I care a lot about our student athletes. I care a lot about our students. And so, I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness," he said. JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY' He also addressed perhaps his most controversial statement, which he made in 2021, while opposing a Texas bill to keep men out of women’s sports. Talarico said on the state House floor that "God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary." "I was being provocative with that statement. I get that," Talarico admitted, explaining, "What I was trying to say is that you can't use human categories to define God, and that's not controversial theologically." Regarding his past comment about there being more than two genders, Talarico said he does not currently believe there are six sexes. "I've missed the mark on some of my past statements. I will be the first to admit it," he said. "What I meant is that there are two sexes, and then there's a small percentage of people with genetic abnormalities." "Obviously didn't say it correctly. There are not six sexes. There are two, and I think the reason that politicians in that convention center across the street want to talk about six sexes is because they don't want to talk about $6 diesel," he said. Though he walked back these controversies, Talarico did not hold back on his criticism of the Supreme Court, which he described as "infected" with corruption, saying it "needs to be overhauled." LONGTIME GOP AIDE DEFECTS TO DEM RISING STAR AS TEXAS SENATE BATTLE FOR CORNYN'S SEAT HEATS UP He said that if elected, "You're going to expect that I will vote for overhaul to the Supreme Court. That will include binding codes of conduct for our justices. It'll include term limits, and I am open to a discussion about expanding the number of justices." Following these controversies, Talarico pledged to keep his message focused on affordability for the remainder of the campaign. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Everywhere I go across the state of Texas, people are struggling to survive in this economy. They are struggling to afford the basics: groceries, gas, utilities, healthcare. And that's what I'm going to be focused on from now until Election Day." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On the topic of affordability, Talarico said that "we should not have a state income tax" in Texas. This is despite Talarico previously voting against a measure to permanently ban a state income tax, which he suggested was redundant and an example of "government waste at its worst." The measure was ultimately passed by the Texas Legislature and approved by Texas voters in November 2019. He knocked Paxton as "the most corrupt politician in Texas," saying, "He's going to try to clip some of my comments, including comments where I was being a little provocative in order to try to distract from that career." Fox News Digital reached out to the Paxton campaign for a response.

news.title: Kevin Reddington says Lindsay Clancy is ‘disappointed’ about mistrial, has ‘love’ for jury
news.text:
BOSTON (WHDH) - In a new sit-down interview with CNN, Lindsay Clancy’s Defense Attorney’ Kevin Reddington said his client is disappointed by the mistrial declared in her murder trial. 

“Disappointed, I mean she absolutely just has such strong feelings for these jurors knowing what they went through several weeks out of their lives, and the work they put into the case, and she just had such great respect, and quite frankly, love for them,” Reddington said.

The jury was unable to unanimously agree on whether Clancy is criminally responsible for killing her three young children in January 2023. 

“She is well aware of the loss of her children, she is well aware of the circumstances of the psychosis,” Reddington said. “And this is the thing that people have difficulty understanding is that when you’re talking about postpartum psychosis, you can be in a psychotic state, you can communicate with people, you can talk on the telephone, you can drive a car, you can make a phone call, you can use Google all of that.”

Reddington’ says he is open to a plea bargain for Clancy, and that she does not deserve prison time.

“She had the sad situation where she was anxious and had to see a doctor, and happened to see this doctor in September of 2022, put her on the medications and she ended up being in a spiral,” Reddington said. “She was improperly prescribed, wasn’t just overprescribed – she was improperly prescribed.”

Reddington was also asked about his plea to President Donald Trump to pardon Clancy.

“I know that it’s not a situation where it’s a federal case, but he does have the Department of Justice behind, he does have an awful lot of club,” Reddington said.

He went on to speak about Lindsay’s then-husband Patrick Clancy, and what he wants the general public to know.

“This is a young couple that was on top of the world. They had three beautiful children, they had a nice house in a beautiful town, they were respected in their jobs, and it just went sideways because of the horrid, horrible, medical, psychiatric care that they had,” Reddington said. “And he stood by her; went to the doctor’s appointments with her, stood by her, testified for her in this trial, and also forgave her which is most important in her mind.”

news.title: 'Passage of time must never dim': Trump renews ‘Never Forget’ vow on 9/11 anniversary
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 10 (IANS) President Donald Trump has proclaimed September 11 (Friday) as Patriot Day, marking the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks that killed 2,977 people in New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania. “A quarter of a century has passed since the terrible day of September 11, 2001, and an entire generation of Americans has now come of age with no living memory of that fateful day,” Trump said in a White House proclamation issued on Wednesday (local time). He called for the promise to remember the victims and the events of that day to be renewed across the country. “The passage of time must never dim what will forever burn bright in the conscience of our Nation,” Trump said. “Amid the ashes of Ground Zero, we made a solemn vow to Never Forget -- a vow that must be renewed in every American heart, taught in every classroom, and honoured in every community across our land.” The proclamation recounted how hijackers seized four commercial aircraft on September 11, 2001, and struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. A fourth plane crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers confronted the hijackers. Trump highlighted the actions of the passengers aboard United Airlines Flight 93, including Todd Beamer, who helped lead the effort to retake the aircraft. “In laying down their lives, those 40 patriots transformed a quiet field into hallowed ground -- leaving behind an everlasting testament to the unbreakable will of the American people,” he said. The President also honoured police officers, firefighters, emergency personnel, rescue workers and volunteers who responded to the attacks. Nearly 100 emergency and first responder agencies participated in rescue and evacuation efforts in New York City, according to the proclamation. “The terrorists sought to break our spirit -- they failed. They sought to divide us -- they could not. They sought to make us afraid -- instead, they awakened the mightiest force for justice the world has ever known,” Trump said. He paid tribute to members of the US Armed Forces who served in conflicts following the attacks, including those killed or left with physical and psychological wounds. “Our Nation owes them a debt that can never be repaid,” the President said. Trump said the threat that produced the attacks had not disappeared and called for continued vigilance at home and abroad. He said his administration remained committed to protecting the United States through a policy of “peace through strength”. “We must ensure that the memory of September 11 never fades into history, but remains a living inheritance passed from one generation of Americans to the next,” he said. Trump directed all US departments, agencies and instrumentalities to fly the American flag at half-staff in honour of the 2,977 victims. He also invited state and territorial governors, organisations and individuals to participate in the observance.

news.title: What did Charlie Kirk say and believe? A look back 1 year after death
news.text:
Slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk was known as a passionate debater. 

Before he was killed last year, the Turning Point USA co-founder was a leading voice in the Republican Party. He grew his Phoenix-based conservative group into a political powerhouse. 

That also made him a controversial figure.

The 31-year-old Kirk used his popular podcast to denounce “woke” ideology and promote Christian, conservative beliefs on hot-button issues like abortion. 

He toured the country to debate students on college campuses. Kirk’s provocative stances on race, religion and gender often went viral online, which both grew his profile and made him the subject of controversy. 

Kirk was shot while debating gun violence on the campus of Utah Valley University one year ago, on Sept. 10, 2025. 

Here are some of the beliefs Kirk was known for.

'Free speech' was Kirk’s touchstone

Kirk approached much of his work under the banner of free speech and civic engagement.

He went viral for challenging those who disagreed with him to “prove me wrong.” He accused the left of shying from those conversations.

“It’s OK to hear something you disagree with. You don’t have to run into a safe space,” Kirk said in a 2017 debate with the left-wing commentator Hasan Piker. 

“Why is it that it’s always the leftist activists, whining and protesting and storming stages and pulling fire alarms, and us conservatives, we sit quietly when we hear things we disagree with?”

Cultural progressivism is a 'spreading pathogen'

Kirk likened “woke thinking” to a “spreading pathogen” and said he believed it was a serious threat to the nation. He spoke often about LGBTQ issues and called the trans movement “one of the most destructive social contagions in human history.” 

He told young, gay conservatives that he disagreed with their lifestyle due to his Christian faith but said he welcomed them into the political right.

Kirk supported Trump’s crackdown on gender identity and sparred with California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom over his state’s protections for LGBTQ rights, though the two found common ground in their view that allowing trans women to compete in women’s sports was unfair. 

Kirk was answering a question about how many transgender Americans had committed mass shootings over the past decade when he was killed. Kirk said, “Too many.” The questioner replied there had been five. The person asked Kirk how many mass shooters there had been overall in America during that time, and Kirk replied, “Counting or not counting gang violence?” 

Offline, Kirk and his organization, the GOP heavyweight Turning Point USA, took concrete steps to counter the spread of “woke” thinking.

The group maintains a “Professor Watchlist” of academics who "discriminate against conservative students and advance leftist propaganda in the classroom." Two Turning Point USA affiliates faced charges after harassing a queer Arizona State University professor on that list and eventually admitted guilt.

Gun deaths ‘worth it’ to protect Second Amendment

Kirk was a staunch supporter of the Second Amendment, which protects the right to bear arms in the United States. 

He opposed new gun regulations and instead advocated for reducing gun violence by “having more fathers in the home” and “having more armed guards in front of schools.” 

He acknowledged during a Turning Point Faith event in 2023 that if Americans were armed, gun deaths never would reach zero. 

“You will never live in a society where you have an armed citizenry and you won’t have a single gun death,” Kirk said. “I think it's worth it. I think it's worth to have a cost of, unfortunately, some gun deaths every single year so that we can have the Second Amendment to protect our other God-given rights. That is a prudent deal. It is rational.” 

Kirk: Civil Rights Act was 'a mistake'

In recent years, Kirk had taken aim at the country’s landmark civil rights legislation.

"I have a very, very radical view on this, but I can defend it, and I've thought about it," Kirk told the crowd at his annual conservative political conference, AmericaFest, in 2023. "We made a huge mistake when we passed the Civil Rights Act in the 1960s." 

It was a refrain Kirk would return to often in public remarks and on his social media talk show. He argued the bill “created a beast” focused on equality of outcomes rather than equality of opportunity, and that it “led to more crime.”

The law outlawed racial segregation in public places, schools and federally assisted programs, and it banned job discrimination. It is credited with helping to reduce stark employment inequality in the United States, along with other major federal civil rights laws passed later in the decade.

Kirk also attacked Martin Luther King Jr., calling the civil rights activist “awful” and “not a good person.”

The topic “would have been even more forbidden four or five years ago” but is now accepted “in more and more mainstream circles,” Kirk said.

American left has 'always hated this country'

Though he quibbled with rivals on the right, Charlie Kirk reserved his harshest criticism for the American left, which he said wanted to “deconstruct our country from within.”

"One of the things that Donald Trump has done is he has not changed the left — he has revealed them," Kirk said at the Conservative Political Action Conference in 2019. "This is who they have always been. They have always hated this country."

He denounced socialism as an “evil, greedy, self-righteous ideology” and characterized the left as engaged in a long march to erode American institutions, including U.S. democracy, marriage and the nuclear family.

Kirk was fiercely anti-abortion

Kirk was a devout Christian who was almost entirely against abortion. 

He discussed his view that “abortion is not a victimless crime” in a 2024 debate against liberal college students. A debate opponent asked Kirk if he had a 10-year-old daughter who was raped and impregnated, whether he’d want her to carry the baby to term. 

“The answer is yes. The baby would be delivered,” Kirk said, calling her question “awfully graphic.” 

Kirk said there was no difference between a baby conceived by rape or by a loving couple. “It’s all human rights and it’s all human beings,” he said. 

“The worst thing to do to the daughter is to then say ‘Hey, we’re going to murder the being inside of you,’” Kirk said. 

Kirk said he supported abortion in only rare situations where the mother’s life was at risk. But Kirk cast doubt on even those cases, saying “it is a growing consensus in the pro-life world that abortion is never medically necessary.” 

Medical professionals disagree with that view. Abortion can be medically necessary, according to The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.

Kirk opposed immigration, 'pockets of culture' within US

Kirk supported Trump’s campaign against undocumented migrants and called for a highly restrictive immigration policy, even opposing forms of legal immigration.

His criticism went beyond policy. The United States should have one culture, he said on a livestream in August 2025: “Americanism."

“We have one culture that you assimilate towards. One. We should not put up with all these different pockets of culture,” Kirk said. 

“America was at its peak when we halted immigration for 40 years and we dropped our foreign-born percentage to its lowest level ever. We should be unafraid to do that,” he said. 

“We have 55 million foreigners in this country, and I'm sure many of them are wonderful people. … But we've got to take a step back and say, guys, that you're no longer a nation. You're something else. You're a colony.”

news.title: Jay Feely praises Trump and free markets in midterm convention speech
news.text:
Republican candidate Jay Feely praised President Donald Trump and free markets during brief remarks at the Republican Party's midterm national convention in Dallas.

Feely, who is running in Arizona's battleground 1st Congressional District, spent most of his five-minute speaking slot lauding small government, low regulation and other economic themes that animated Republicans in the years before Trump's ascent.

He also told the crowd that the attempted 2024 assassination of Trump is what motivated him to step away from his work as a sports commentator and run for political office.

"With blood on his face, President Trump raised a fist and he told this nation to fight," Feely told the crowd. "I walked away from a dream job to get off the sidelines and into that fight."

The so-called "Trumpapalooza" event had divided Republican candidates in swing congressional districts. The White House's low approval ratings have appeared to drag on the GOP ticket, and some strategists have questioned the decision to emphasize the president's political brand in the run-up to the election.

The Republican incumbent in Arizona's other battleground congressional district, Rep. Juan Ciscomani, told a Washington, D.C., publication he would prioritize a Sept. 10 televised debate against his Democratic challenger rather than attend Trump's convention.

Feely appeared onstage alongside Mike Bouchard Jr., the GOP nominee in one of Michigan's swing districts, and briefly mentioned Feely's Democratic opponent, former state Rep. Amish Shah.

Shah was known for his bipartisan approach to governance at the Arizona Legislature, and his platform places him toward the ideological center of his party. That hasn't stopped Feely's allies from calling Shah a "Democrat socialist" in television attack ads across the district, a line Feely repeated from the Sept. 9 convention stage.

Feely invoked former President Ronald Reagan to tell the crowd that "freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction."

"We will not surrender our future. We are the ones that must preserve it," he said.

Shah's campaign took the opportunity to highlight his work as an emergency room doctor.

"While my opponent is pledging his loyalty to Donald Trump in Dallas, I'm in the ER taking care of Arizonans," he wrote on social media.

news.title: Letter from Doonbeg: The calm before a different storm
news.text:
In true Irish fashion, the fine china is out and the dust has been swept under the carpet for the arriving guests. Signs to herald nearby coffee trucks with their enticing toasties have been repainted. Local filling stations are bedecked with balloon arches. It all screams calculated hospitality.

There is a palpable warmth in its people. The number of Garda personnel all over the county is staggering. Stewards and volunteers will help approximately 75,000 patrons find their way to a course that is only accessible by park-and-ride, with even pedestrian access prohibited.

A special nod to Dominic Sullivan of Kilkee for his timely assistance in removing some stubborn wheel nuts on our punctured tyre this week. The real heroes are the ones on the other side of the rope, ensuring the clumsy aren’t trapped in a waterlogged field for hours upon hours.

On the flip side, we have the circus. US President Donald Trump’s shadow here was inevitable once the venue was selected. The club’s management expect protests, while the added security apparatus is unmissable. The old gift shop has been converted into a makeshift office for various attendees to collect additional accreditation via Garda vetting. It’s that kind of week.

It hangs over every element of this event. There is every chance play will have to be stopped on Saturday to facilitate his helicopters’ arrival. Rory McIlroy and Shane Lowry are among the favourites, along with the likes of Jon Rahm, Robert MacIntyre and Tyrrell Hatton. What part will Trump play in the trophy presentation? How will those potential images age? Is the inconvenience worth the spectacle?

Well, that depends. Golfer after golfer walked off the course early in the week and reached for the same links cliché: these wide fairways and soft greens are eminently scoreable if the weather is calm. If the wind picks up and howls, it’ll become a brutal challenge. The layout encourages players to get their scoring done early and then hold on down the back nine.

Doonbeg is a classic out-and-back course, playing with the wind for the first half. Its reduced field, down from the typical 156, is a necessary measure to complete play, particularly on Thursday and Friday. That layout also means it’s not really feasible to host a two-tee start.

As well as that, you couldn’t describe the rolling undulations as spectator-friendly. There are only 900 grandstand seats, while those brave enough to follow play will face steep coastal dunes. Any casual onlooker may be best off opting for a natural perch on that sweeping amphitheatre that those towering ridges create.

Without demanding conditions, competitors will score here. It wasn’t always this way. At the official opening back in 2002, Pádraig Harrington played Greg Norman in front of 3,000 people. That was when the place was raw and real.

“It was really quirky. Crazy things, crisscrossing holes, bunkers and grains, you could be on the green and couldn't see the pin,” he recalled on Wednesday.

“Like really mad stuff. That is kind of how you imagine a links golf course a hundred years ago was.

“Since Trump has taken over the ownership, it has turned it into a tournament golf course. It has softened up a lot of things and brought things into being a bit, I suppose you would use the word fairer, but certainly more standardised in competitive golf, because you know, the course that we played in 2002, that was crazy.” 

More pleasant for the players. What about everyone else? The sickos among us would prefer to watch toil and struggle, a testament to the true artistry that should come with playing links golf. This conflict is not unique to Doonbeg, but you couldn’t claim the breathtaking scenery poses a legitimate hazard either. There are dunes that wouldn’t even be a consideration for the longest hitters in this field.

Early in the week, the gusts were absolutely relentless. During one practice round, four-time European Tour winner Guido Migliozzi lost a ball at the back of the fourth green. While helping him search, we found two other abandoned balls that had been blown off line in the practice round. His cheerful offer, “whatever you find, you keep,” saw us skipping back with a pocket full of Titleists and TaylorMades. We tell you this to explain the favourable coverage the Italian will likely receive in these pages for the rest of the week.

As for the geo-politics, golf is a sport that has spent decades trying to feel less like a corporate enterprise and more like something authentic. It has been remarkable to watch the Irish golfers responsible for advancing the game here, who fuelled its popularity through their own relatability, try to navigate uncomfortable questions about the looming presence over the past few days. There is no separating the sport from the political sideshow at a venue like this. The only guarantee for this tournament is that the escapism of sport will be overruled by the real world.
news.summary: There is no separating the sport from the political sideshow at a venue like this. The only guarantee for this tournament is that the escapism of sport will be overruled by the real world

news.title: Paul Pelosi’s Bloom trade blossoms — what a surprise
news.text:
Nancy and Paul Pelosi’s amazing track record of picking stocks continues.

In July, the power couple bought shares of Bloom Energy, a controversial “green” energy company, right after a sharp drop in price, and right before an upbeat earnings report.

And then — surprise! — the company’s stock took off, especially after the company was admitted to the elite list of companies tracked by the S&P 500 index.

The former speaker has denied allegations of insider trading for years, saying she leaves trades to her husband. 

Paul Pelosi is evidently a stock market savant. That would be the same Paul Pelosi who keeps getting into trouble with the law for his errant driving, including a recent hit-and-run misdemeanor charge.

The Pelosi trades weren’t just small transactions, either. In several trades over several days, they bought at least $3 million worth of shares and options. 

They must have been really, really confident.

Maybe they were just looking at the fact that Bloom Energy has skyrocketed in the last year. 

It hovered below $20 per share until last summer, as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom took off, and investors realized that all those data centers were going to need some new energy sources.

Bloom Energy’s “boxes” use hydrogen fuel cells to generate power. But fuel cells have been one of many disappointing “green” alternatives — until recently.

Perhaps the company’s promise of clean, abundant power is finally coming true just as demand is rising.

It can’t hurt that the company has long had ties to the Silicon Valley elite — and the political elite. 

The Pelosi stock trades could be completely legitimate.

But they renew questions about whether one of the most powerful political leaders in Washington has used her position and her access to information to cash in on opportunities not available to other Americans.

In 2011, journalists raised questions about how Paul Pelosi had managed to buy 5,000 shares of Visa at its IPO price. Later, in 2024, ethics groups questioned Pelosi’s decision to sell $500,000 worth of Visa stock right before the company was sued by the U.S. Department of Justice.

Nancy Pelosi has long resisted efforts to restrict stock trades by members of Congress and their spouses.

She won the gavel in the 2006 midterm elections promising to “drain the swamp” — a promise later recycled by Donald Trump.

Twenty years later, she is leaving Washington in a rather swampy way.

news.title: 'This was a war:' How 9/11 changed George W. Bush's presidency and legacy
news.text:
WASHINGTON – President George W. Bush had been seated in front of a classroom of Florida second graders for just five minutes when White House Chief of Staff Andy Card rushed over and whispered an urgent message in his ear: "America is under attack."

In an instant, the world – and Bush’s nascent presidency – had changed.

The assault on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on the clear-blue morning of Sept. 11, 2001, along with the crash of a hijacked plane in Pennsylvania that day, killed nearly 3,000 people and shattered Americans’ sense of safety in the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil.

For Bush, who had been in office just eight months, the attacks would be the defining moment of his presidency.

“There was no doubt in my mind that this was not a law-enforcement event. This was a war,” Bush said at an event at his presidential center in Dallas on Sept. 9 to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

Bush “didn't sign up to become a wartime president, but you became one," Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said at the Dallas event. “Leadership starts at the top.”

The events of 9/11 altered the trajectory of Bush’s legacy.

In his first few months in office, Bush had been focused mostly on domestic concerns, such as education reform. After 9/11, he abruptly shifted to soothing a traumatized nation and keeping Americans safe – a priority that would lead to two wars, changes in the government’s domestic security operations, and a sweeping antiterrorism campaign that continues to this day.

His former staffers recalled, in an oral history project by the University of Virginia’s Miller Center, how the 9/11 attacks and their aftermath influenced their work for the remainder of Bush’s presidency.

Coping with wounds: 25 years later, these 9/11 survivors still carry the scars

"So many people we spoke to said, 'You have to understand that for us, both in terms of policy and how the presidency changed overnight with that first plane hitting the World Trade Center, every day for us was like 9/12,'" said Barbara Perry, cochair of the Miller Center’s Presidential Oral History Program.

Bush entered the White House after winning an election so close that it triggered a 36-day recount in Florida, halted only by a divided Supreme Court. But in the days following 9/11, his popularity soared as Americans rallied around their new leader. A week after the attacks, his approval rating jumped to 90% in a Gallup poll, the highest ever recorded.

Some of the most unforgettable images of Bush’s eight years in office were captured on 9/11 and the days and weeks after. One of the most famous is the moment Card interrupted his appearance at a classroom in Sarasota, Florida, as a child read a book out loud. A look of bewilderment washed over Bush's face.

"I didn't have much time to process that," Bush recalled in Dallas, "but it was pretty clear to me that if we were under attack, then my job was to defend the child that was reading to me and her family and her country."

Another indelible moment came three days later when Bush stood atop a crumpled firetruck amid the rubble of the twin towers in New York and used a bullhorn to address first responders digging through the debris. When someone yelled they couldn’t hear him, Bush replied with a message that was part rallying cry and part warning to the perpetrators of the attacks.

"I can hear you," he said. "The rest of the world hears you. And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon."

To reassure a shaken nation, Bush said he took on the role of "comforter-in-chief because I had a sense that there was a lot of trauma. I didn't want us to lose our soul."

Three weeks after Bush's bullhorn moment, the United States and its allies launched a military campaign against Afghanistan and its ruling Taliban regime. The goal was to destroy the al-Qaida terrorist network responsible for the attacks and to track down its leader, Osama bin Laden, who was hiding in caves in the country’s mountainous terrain. Bin Laden, however, would remain elusive until 2011, when a U.S. Navy SEAL Team killed him during a raid on his Pakistan compound.

Meanwhile, Bush convinced Congress to pass the USA Patriot Act, which gave law enforcement and intelligence agencies greater surveillance and investigative powers, including the use of roving wiretaps to track communications across multiple devices. The law also made it easier for law enforcement to monitor domestic and international phone calls and email.

In addition, Bush created a new Cabinet position, the Department of Homeland Security, which merged nearly two dozen federal departments and agencies into one organization. Before, the different groups often failed to share information, creating dangerous gaps in the nation's security apparatus.

Some of Bush's actions were controversial, including a secretive executive order he signed that allowed the National Security Agency to intercept phone calls and emails of U.S. citizens without a warrant. Critics argued the order was an illegal overreach of executive power and violated civil liberties.

'Two sides of the same coin': A 12-year-old lost his father in 9/11. What he’s learned since

Bush’s most controversial decision, though, was invading Iraq in 2003. His administration linked Iraq and its leader, Saddam Hussein, to al-Qaida and the 9/11 attacks, even though U.S. intelligence agencies concluded Iraq had nothing to do with either. Hussein had used chemical weapons in the past, and the Bush administration argued he had stockpiled weapons of mass destruction that could be used against the United States and its allies.

No such weapons were ever found. Bush’s popularity tanked. Public opinion turned against the war, which would not end until late 2011 – nearly three years after he left office.

Final moments: Why this photographer’s 9/11 ‘Falling Man’ photo remains controversial

In the years since, the American public has begun to reassess Bush’s legacy, said Perry of the University of Virginia’s Presidential Oral History Program. 

"By comparison and contrast to Donald Trump, who doesn’t always seem like the best representative of the United States in the world, I think people will give Bush credit for not allowing another attack on the homeland," Perry said.

But Bush’s record on national security must be balanced against leading the nation into two wars in which more than 7,000 American service members were killed and thousands of others were wounded, she said.

The Taliban’s return to power in 2021 in Afghanistan, following the collapse of the U.S.-backed government, "does not help Bush’s long-term legacy, nor does the Iraq war that I think most people think was unnecessary," Perry said.

In Dallas, Bush said 9/11 had been “a clarifying moment” for him and others in his administration because they realized "we were vulnerable to attack based on what we believe.”

"I felt like bringing al-Qaida to justice was honoring the families of the fallen,” he said.

news.title: Global goods trade strengthening: WTO
news.text:
GENEVA: Global trade in goods has strengthened from June despite geopolitical and policy-related uncertainties, the World Trade Organization said on Wednesday, signalling resilience in merchandise flows even as risks remain elevated.

The September reading of the WTO’s barometer tracking merchandise trade growth was 102, an improvement from the June barometer of 101.7, with growth remaining above trend.

The WTO publishes its Goods Trade Barometer four times a year. It covers export orders, air freight, container shipping, automotive products, raw materials and electronic components.

Readings above 100 indicate growth above the baseline trend of 100, while figures below 100 point to below-trend growth.

The Geneva-based trade body said the strengthening came despite uncertainty linked to geopolitical tensions and trade policy developments.

In March, the WTO forecast that growth in world trade in goods would slow down markedly to 1.9% this year from 4.6% in 2025 and could decelerate even more if the US war with Iran continues to push up energy prices and disrupt global transport.

US President Donald Trump has imposed sweeping tariffs on global trading partners, while shipping through the key Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil supplies used to transit, has been severely disrupted by conflict in the Middle East.

However, strong demand for electronic components tied to investment in AI and digital infrastructure was helping offset the negative effects from those factors, the WTO report said.

Trade growth remains uneven across sectors and regions, and the WTO warned that geopolitical and policy-related risks continue to cloud the outlook due to ongoing disruption to supply chains, shipping routes and transport costs.
