news.title: The shock has stopped shocking
news.text:
Perhaps the strangest thing about Brent crossing $100 again is how unsurprising it has begun to feel. Six months into the Iran war, traders are still trying to establish how much oil is actually moving through the Strait of Hormuz, tankers are disappearing from tracking systems, attacks are spreading towards alternative export routes, and a geopolitical premium appears increasingly embedded in energy prices. Yet the global economy continues expanding, investors remain remarkably willing to take risk and policymakers increasingly discuss disruption as though it were simply another variable to feed into their models.

Could this be what analysts are beginning to call the “new, new normal”?

There was a time when roughly 20 million barrels of oil passing through Hormuz every day was one of those facts markets barely needed to think about. That certainty has vanished. The US administration claimed more than 17 million barrels crossed under naval supervision on August 31. Kpler, an energy-data firm that tracks global oil flows using satellite imagery, vessel signals, port records, and shipping intelligence, put the figure at perhaps six million barrels. More recent industry data has put flows below two million barrels per day. Tankers increasingly travel “dark”, satellite visibility has been reduced, and competing American and Iranian restrictions have turned the world’s most important energy artery into something approaching a statistical guessing game.

How exactly does an oil market price supply when it cannot confidently measure it?

Apparently, by putting a price on uncertainty itself. Brent breached $100 on Wednesday for the first time since July, having risen roughly a quarter since early August as hopes for a durable settlement faded. Attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi energy facilities are now threatening the Red Sea route that helped compensate for severely curtailed Hormuz traffic. Banks have been lifting crude-price forecasts, while markets increasingly appear to be pricing a prolonged conflict rather than another temporary disruption.

And how much of this new normal owes to Donald Trump’s original blunder in allowing Benjamin Netanyahu’s Iran gamble to pull Washington into a war that was supposed to settle matters rather more cleanly? Six months later, the result is repeated military escalation, severely disrupted energy flows and a Strait of Hormuz whose normal functioning can no longer be taken for granted. Brent reached $126.41 at its April peak, fell back when hopes of settlement returned and has now climbed through $100 once more. Perhaps the more important development is no longer the occasional spike in crude, but the possibility that geopolitical insecurity is acquiring a semi-permanent price of its own.

That possibility becomes more troubling because crude is only part of the story. Refined-product markets are also tightening pretty sharply. Diesel supply has been squeezed by disruptions to Middle Eastern and Russian exports, while limited spare refining capacity makes replacement difficult. US diesel prices have reached record levels, gasoline is climbing, inventories are already depleted and refinery maintenance season is approaching. Hedge funds, which spent the early months of the war largely bearish, have swung aggressively bullish on gasoline and diesel even while remaining comparatively cautious on crude. So, could the next energy shock therefore arrive at the refinery rather than the wellhead?

The wider economic backdrop makes that question particularly awkward. Despite two wars, expensive energy and sharply higher borrowing costs, global growth is running surprisingly hot. JPMorgan’s global business surveys showed activity rising for a fifth consecutive month in August to its strongest level in more than two years, consistent with annualised global GDP growth of 3.1 percent against the bank’s estimate of 2.3 percent potential growth. AI investment, defence spending and corporate capital expenditure are keeping demand strong even as supply disruptions add inflationary pressure.

What happens when unusually strong demand collides with structurally more expensive energy? Central banks may be about to find out. Governments, already carrying historically heavy debt burdens, appear reluctant to restrain fiscal policy because many are relying on growth itself to stabilise debt ratios. That leaves monetary policy increasingly responsible for applying the brakes. Higher-for-longer interest rates then begin looking less like an unpleasant interlude and more like another feature of the emerging landscape.

For Pakistan, there is very little theoretical about any of this. Inflation is rising again after the relief of the earlier disinflation cycle, while economic growth has for years struggled to create enough space for a rapidly expanding population. Now oil is threatening another sustained climb precisely as daily fuel-price revisions transmit international movements much faster to consumers. The pain does not remain confined to the filling station. Diesel moves trucks, tractors and generators; higher transport costs work their way through vegetables, grain, manufactured goods and almost everything else that must travel from producer to consumer.

Then comes the external account. Pakistan imports much of its energy requirement, so a persistent geopolitical premium on crude feeds directly into the import bill, the currency equation and eventually inflation. At the same time, the same forces keeping energy expensive are helping keep global interest rates elevated. An economy can therefore find itself paying more for oil and more for capital at precisely the moment when domestic households and businesses are least equipped to absorb either.

So what exactly does “normalisation” mean for a country caught between dearer energy, dearer money and weak underlying growth?

Perhaps Brent slips back below $100. Perhaps Hormuz flows recover. Perhaps diplomacy eventually achieves what six months of warfare have failed to deliver. Markets have spent much of this conflict repeatedly betting on such outcomes. Yet the more uncomfortable question is whether the benchmark itself has changed.

If oil traders must routinely price invisible tankers, naval escorts, alternative shipping corridors, refinery shortages and the possibility of another missile strike; if central banks must price geopolitical inflation alongside unusually strong demand; and if downstream economies such as Pakistan must absorb those costs with ever shorter lags, what exactly are we expecting to return to?

Maybe “normal service” is the wrong thing to wait for.

news.title: Bessent backs using US financial power as foreign policy tool
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent advocated on Tuesday for Washington’s use of financial power as a foreign policy tool with the goal of advancing the interests of American allies, including in financial and political situations abroad.

“I believe that I can use the balance sheet of the US for foreign policy. So, we have a foreign policy goal and that is to create allies in the Western hemisphere,” Bessent said in an event at the SMU Cox School of Business.

“Argentina was the front-runner for that and it was my belief that the Milei government had sound policies,” he said, referring to Argentine President Javier Milei’s government.

Last year, the US provided Argentina with a multibillion-dollar support package to help stabilize its currency and bolster Milei ahead of midterm elections.

Bessent’s comments marked an open acknowledgment of the Trump administration’s willingness to use US financial resources to shape the politics and economies of foreign countries.

President Donald Trump’s administration has tried to sway political contests across other parts of Latin America and has moved to increase US presence and influence in the region.

Trump also ordered the seizure of ousted Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in a deadly raid and the US military has carried out multiple strikes on boats in the Caribbean that have killed dozens.

Rights advocates, both in the US and around the world, say such actions are imperialist and amount to extrajudicial killings. Trump casts them as attempts to advance US interests and counter drug trafficking and illegal immigration.

Bessent also spoke about the US having joined Japan in a rare joint yen-buying intervention on July 31, which signalled determination to prevent a selloff in the yen and Japanese government bonds from spilling over into global markets.

“When we intervened with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Japanese, what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policy makers are going to do,” Bessent said.

The Financial Times reported that the Treasury chief cautioned market participants that challenging his interventions could invite pain. “I have asymmetric information. I am the house now,” the newspaper said Bessent said at the event, adding “you can bet against me if you want.”

Despite Bessent’s confidence in the direction of his interventions, which have included actions to counter a rise in long-term government bond yields, the real world impact-has been mixed. The yen has rallied amid Middle East war developments and was at a seven-month high Wednesday amid pressure on the dollar.

Meanwhile, the government’s long-term borrowing costs have risen despite the Treasury’s desire for that not to happen. On Wednesday the government announced upsized buyback operations for long-dated Treasuries, while the yield on the 30-year bond moved up to its highest level since 2007.

The 10-year bond yield, which is highly influential in setting real-world borrowing costs, is also up quite a bit. The 30-year mortgage rates rose in the latest week, hitting their highest level since June 2025 at 6.85% in the week ended September 4, the Mortgage Bankers Association said on Wednesday.

news.title: Donald Trump’s Irish Open – is the baggage worth the eyeballs?
news.text:
“I think when the sitting President of the United States of America visits anywhere, it becomes a logistical challenge,” said defending champion Rory McIlroy at his press conference.

“There's a lot that goes into it. They obviously have to lock down a specific area and make sure that it's safe for him to travel into, and the entire delegation, whoever that is. Logistically, it provides a bit of a challenge, but we are at one of his properties that he has kindly provided for us to play a golf tournament.

“I said yesterday, the President of the United States wants to come watch a little bit of golf. I think we are all happy to be here, grateful to be here. His presence at The Irish Open makes it a truly international event. That brings more attention and eyeballs to The Irish Open and it can only be a good thing.” 

In an interview with the Irish Independent earlier this year, Eric Trump, the son of the US president, hailed McIlroy as a friend and said that without his support, the tournament likely would not have taken place in Doonbeg.

Learn more “Eric and I live very close to each other, kids are at the same school and see each other at school events from time to time,” explained McIlroy when asked about their relationship.

“So the DP World Tour reached out to me and said, ‘Do you think Doonbeg will be a suitable venue for The Irish Open?’ “I said, look, I haven't been there, but from all accounts, I hear it's a very, very good golf course with accommodation on-site. The Irish Open has not been in this part of the world in several years, since Lahinch in 2019. I think it would be a good thing.”

The security detail is considerable this week, but the players themselves have their own priorities. Their focus is on the course itself.

“For the players, every player here, is absolutely a hundred percent focused on trying to play their best golf,” said Pádraig Harrington.

“There are a lot of different stories for the players. Some guys trying to get into the Ryder Cup team. Some guys trying to keep their cards. Players are very good at just managing, because we travel all around the world. There's always stuff going on.

“You know, it is a huge deal, a sitting US President coming in. I've met both Bushes. Played golf with Bill Clinton; that was really cool. I've met Obama, obviously, at the White House for St. Patrick's Day. I met President Trump back in the day, before he was President.

“It is a huge deal with a US President coming in. There’s going to be a huge focus. The place looks fantastic. It looks brilliant. There's a lot of attention and some of that attention is good and bad attention, there is no doubt about it.” 

Protests are expected this weekend, with several activist groups set to take part in a demonstration called ‘The Great Irish Unwelcome’. Trump originally bought the resort in 2014 after the venue was put into receivership.

“Obviously politically, there's a different side to this, and it is exceptionally complicated,” said Harrington.

“I play my golf in the US and it is exceptionally complicated in the US, let alone coming over here.

“You know, everybody, there are a lot of opinions. My friends will be on both sides of the counter. It is very topical and a difficult one because as I said, I have good friends who are on both sides and they are still good friends.

“So it's much easier from a golfing perspective. He does a really good golf course and a really good venue. The attention, as I said, for this tournament, it's putting all eyes here, and the people at Doonbeg, it's going to make this venue a bigger place. The jobs and economy, they are going to do great.

“He does a good golf course. The political side is certainly a hot potato for when you discuss it.” 

Boil it down and their message is simple: let us play golf. Even that will be further complicated by the fact that play may need to be halted. If Marine One touches down while play is ongoing, there may be a delay.

“Look, is it a little disruptive to play? Absolutely,” admitted McIlroy.

“But again, there are protocols in place for a reason, and all we can do is follow them and abide by them, and whenever we're ready to play again, we put our heads down and we go and play.”

Some balked at high attendance fees. Republican House members were being asked to pay $25,000 for convention tickets and lodging, according to people familiar with the situation and granted anonymity to speak frankly about the private arrangement.

An additional 2,000 tickets were distributed by the National Republican Congressional Committee, largely to donors and others to attend the convention. Other tickets were allocated to state parties to distribute as they saw fit.

Democrats have held such midterm conventions in the past but are not doing so this year. Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said she wasn’t worried that her party was missing an opportunity to make its case on a national stage like Republicans.

news.title: Shocking new life of CIA's 'Queen of Torture' who hunted Al-Qaeda and inspired beloved movie: Neighbors reveal ugly local whispers... as truth Hollywood edited out returns to haunt her
news.text:
The CIA's notorious 'Queen of Torture' spent much of her career hunting down national security threats and watching on as screaming Al Qaeda suspects were waterboarded in secret prisons amid the war on terror. 

But now, the fierce red-headed spy agency analyst who inspired Jessica Chastain's role in the Hollywood blockbuster Zero Dark Thirty has been quietly rebranding herself as a life coach deep in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley. 

Years after leading the CIA unit that was built to destroy Al Qaeda, Alfreda Frances Bikowsky – as she was once known – is living the quiet life in a stately brick Georgian with sweeping Blue Ridge views as she doles out life advice to women. 

These days, the 61-year-old goes by Freda Scheuer – and is unsurprisingly reluctant to talk about her past life some five years after retiring from clandestine service. 

Reached at her home ahead of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks that defined her career, Scheuer declined to speak to the Daily Mail. 

'I am afraid I must respectfully decline,' she said, citing the spate of critical media coverage of her over the years. 

Scheuer – dubbed by her fiercest critics simply as the 'Torture Queen' – has been blamed for dropping the ball before the 9/11 attacks, misreading intelligence, defending brutal interrogations of suspects who were sometimes innocent and lying to Congress about whether any of it worked. 

But neighbors near the two-acre spread Scheuer shares with her husband, former CIA officer Michael Scheuer, said she now largely keeps to herself.

'I wouldn't recognize either of them if they knocked on my door and showed up for dinner,' one neighbor told us. 

Another said they want nothing to do with the 'spook' down the street: 'That lady has too many skeletons in her closet to be any kind of self-help guru.' 

Scheuer, who grew up in small-town Pennsylvania and was the first in her family to go to college, joined the CIA as a security analyst in the 1990s. She later signed on in 1999 with the unit tasked with hunting Osama bin Laden – an office founded by Michael Scheuer, the man she'd marry 15 years later.

'I wanted to be at a place where I could earn my seat at the table and make a difference, have it count,' she said recently on the Ok Sweetie podcast.

She quickly rose through the ranks, becoming deputy chief of the unit and then its chief by 2003. 

Hollywood painted her as brilliant and relentless in her quest to fight terror – but her real record is arguably uglier. 

According to government reports, she failed to warn anyone that one of her underlings knew two Al-Quaeda operatives who would go on to become the 9/11 hijackers – Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi – had entered the US.

The CIA never told the FBI or the State Department. Both men were aboard Flight 77 when it hit the Pentagon on 9/11. Critics say the intel might not have stopped the attack but that it could have blunted it.

Scheuer has long denied allegations that she withheld the information because of tensions with the FBI. 

She insisted she personally hand-delivered the visa information to the bureau, although no evidence ever backed her up. The 9/11 Commission, which was set up in the wake of the attacks, effectively called her account false.

Asked more recently if she felt guilty about 9/11, she shrugged it off, saying in the recent podcast interview: 'To be honest, I don't think I even had time for guilt. Wasting time, crying over, you know, it happened… I did my best.'

Even as colleagues questioned her judgment, she kept climbing as one of the few analysts who knew al-Qaeda inside and out. She was determined not to let another terrorist slip through her fingers. Critics have said that determination curdled into an obsession.

In 2002, an officer believed to be Scheuer made a point of personally watching the interrogation of Abu Zubaydah, a man wrongly branded a 9/11 planner, according to a Senate report. 

As the first detainee subjected to the CIA's newly designed 'enhanced interrogation techniques,' he was waterboarded more than 80 times in a single month, confined in a coffin-sized 'dog box,' subjected to sleep deprivation and prolonged isolation, and lost an eye while being interrogated, the report added. 

A year later, according to Jane Mayer's book The Dark Side, a similarly described officer flew to a black site at taxpayer expense just to watch Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind behind the attacks, get waterboarded. 

Her only reason, a colleague said, was that 'she thought it would be cool to be in the room.'

Mayer later wrote, without naming her, that the officer was behind 'years' worth of terrible judgment.'

Separately, per the Senate Torture Report put out in 2014, an analyst who meets Scheuer's description had interrogators slam Mohammed's head into a wall until he 'confessed' to recruiting black Muslim operatives in Montana. 

It was a lie, extracted by torture, according to the report. US agents wasted weeks chasing ghosts across Big Sky Country – apparently on the unnamed analyst's orders.

Her critics, including Congressional investigators, say her biggest blunder, though, was that involving German car salesman Khaled El-Masri who wound up being drugged, sodomized and tortured for four months at a black site – all because an analyst known only as 'Frances' pushed for his abduction and kept him locked up even after signs showed the CIA had the wrong man.

Government investigators later insisted it should have been clear he was the wrong man. 

While US courts ultimately tossed a lawsuit filed by El-Masri because of national security, the European Court of Human Rights believed his account and slammed the CIA's rendition program for mock executions, stress positions, forced starvation and worse. 

Still, top agency brass brushed off calls to fire her, writing that 'mistakes should be expected in a business filled with uncertainty.' 

She was promoted instead – eventually running the agency's Global Jihad unit. 

Scheuer retired in 2021 with three of the CIA's top honors. 

'She was rewarded for her work and I have been punished as a victim,' El-Masri revealed in a March interview with The New Statesman. 

Scheuer, for her part, bristled at her 'Queen of Torture' nickname and reputation, telling Reuters in a rare 2022 interview that it was sexist.

'I got that title because I was in the arena. In fact, I raised my hand loud and proud and you know, I don't regret it at all,' she said. 

'I never saw anything that constituted torture, period,' she has previously said, adding that her methods '100% saved lives.' 

Scheuer's career has spilled out onto the big screen. 

Hollywood turned her into 'Maya,' played by Jessica Chastain in Zero Dark Thirty, and 'Diane Marsh' in Hulu's miniseries, The Looming Tower. 

She has been adamant in the past, though, that Zero Dark Thirty isn't based on her life – and that it took her years to even watch the film.

Scheuer, who was known inside the CIA for touching up her makeup and applying skin care products mid-meeting, opted for the unusual career shift in 2021 after leaving the CIA. 

She launched a beauty site – YBeUBeauty.com – in 2021, which has since gone dark. 

It has been replaced by a new business, YBeU Life Coaching, which sells 'certified life and leadership coaching' to women – touting her years 'leading teams of mostly women in a high-stakes profession traditionally dominated by men.' 

'Some people think it's pretty unusual to go from being an intelligence officer hunting terrorists, to becoming a life coach,' the site description continues. 

It features a photo of her leaning over her kitchen counter, coffee mug in hand, staring into the camera as if she can read your darkest secret.

Much like the interrogations she once defended, her coaching, which costs $397 for three sessions, appears to push clients past their comfort zones. 

Her Instagram is full of lines like 'Always do what you are afraid to do' and 'Do something every day that scares you.' 

She gushes online, too, about her husband, whom she refers to as 'Mr. YBeU.' 

Since leaving the CIA, Michael Scheuer – who has become a blogger, podcaster and Fox News regular – has taken to espousing conspiracy theories and called on President Donald Trump to impose martial law after he lost the 2020 election, according to Reuters. 

Scheuer, for her part, declined to say if she agreed with her husband's ideas when she gave her Reuters interview – but insisted at the time that she debates him on some issues. 

Now, in light of her rebrand and quiet life in Virginia, human rights advocates insist Freda Scheuer got away with torture. 

'It's disappointing that there has been no accountability,' said John Sifton of Human Rights Watch, who has tracked her for 25 years and worked with detainees tortured during interrogations. 

His warning to Scheuer's would-be life-coach clients: 'You might ask yourself why you'd seek advice from someone who took part in a scandalous program that undermined the credibility of the CIA, the US and the entire counterterrorism framework that was set up after September 11. 

'That legacy will follow her.
news.summary: The CIA's notorious 'Queen of Torture' spent much of her career hunting down national security threats and watching on as screaming Al Qaeda suspects were waterboarded.
news.author: Editor,Susan Greene

news.title: Wait! John Fetterman Spoke at the GOP's Midterm Convention?
news.text:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) is a Democrat. He’s a left-wing Democrat, too. His party is hoping to regain control of Congress so it can can stop Trump’s agenda and impeach him.

Yet he actually spoke at the GOP’s midterm convention Wednesday night.

Fetterman appeared via a prerecorded video to introduce Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) before his speech and praised both McCormick and President Donald Trump for standing up for America's steel industry.

"Yes, I'm Senator John Fetterman, Pennsylvania. Yes, I'm a Democrat," Fetterman said in the video. "Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I'm a common-sense Democrat. I'm always going to stand with America, I'm always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life."

He didn't stop there. Fetterman called McCormick "the kind of senator that gets the job done" and said he was "proud to count him as my friend," despite the two men belonging to opposite parties. Standing near a U.S. steel mill, Fetterman promised to work with Trump "to fight and defend the steel way of life right here in the Steel Valley." Then he turned the floor over to his Republican colleague. "So for everybody in Dallas, I'm here to introduce Dave McCormick," Fetterman said.

Now, obviously, Fetterman isn't exactly riding high with his own party these days. His approval numbers among Pennsylvania Democrats have collapsed, and he’s facing a near-certain Democrat primary challenger when he’s up for reelection in 2028. With fewer than eight weeks left before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, an appearance like this isn’t just a friendly cameo; it's more like a giant middle finger aimed squarely at his own party.

According to a report from Axios, the convention cameo set off a fresh round of speculation over whether Fetterman will ditch the Democrat Party altogether before his 2028 reelection fight. A defection would be a nightmare for Democrats, who need to flip four seats, some in deep-red territory, just to retake the Senate majority.

Related: LIVE Blog: GOP 2026 Midterm Convention, Night One

Of course, I’ve said for a long time now that Fetterman isn't going anywhere. He still votes with Democrats 95% of the time, and his actual policy positions remain solidly on the left. The video functioned as a calculated jab at his own party's socialist drift.

Based John Fetterman 👊🏻 pic.twitter.com/VtEf1Lmw9N— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) September 9, 2026

And the jab landed exactly where the GOP wanted it to. Republicans have spent this election cycle trying to tie the Democrat Party to its socialist wing, and having a sitting Democrat senator vouch for a Republican colleague in a primetime convention video does that work for them. Trump has spent years courting disaffected Democrats, so watching one show up on the GOP's biggest stage of the cycle counts as a win he didn't even have to ask for.

Crossover convention appearances are rare, but they're not unheard of. The late Sen. Zell Miller (D-Ga.) endorsed George W. Bush over John Kerry in 2004 and spoke at that year's Republican convention. The late Sen. Joe Lieberman (D-Conn.) went from being the Democrats' vice presidential nominee in 2000 to speaking at John McCain's GOP convention in 2008, because he viewed Barack Obama as too radical and dangerous for the country. And in 2024, Tulsi Gabbard, a former Democrat presidential candidate, endorsed Trump and spoke at the Republican convention herself.

Fetterman's cameo fits that same pattern: a Democrat willing to say, on camera, that his own party has drifted too far to trust. Make no mistake about it, the rest of the country just watched one of their senators make the GOP's argument for them, and that was awesome.

news.title: Fetterman Makes Shock RNC Speech as PA Republicans Say Switch Not Needed
news.text: Democratic Senator John Fetterman made a surprise appearance at the Republican midterm convention Wednesday, vowing to work with President Donald Trump on Pennsylvania steel as he introduced Republican Senator Dave McCormick in a prerecorded video. Newsweek National Political Correspondent Alex Rouhandeh, who attended, said Fetterman drew big cheers from the Pennsylvania delegation, which stood and applauded as the video concluded. “Yes, I'm a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I'm a common-sense Democrat,” Fetterman said. Newsweek reached out to the Democratic National Committee via email for comment. Fetterman has become increasingly isolated from members of his own party while drawing praise from Republicans, fueling speculation that he could eventually switch parties. Fetterman has repeatedly said he remains a Democrat. “I'm always going to stand with America. I'm always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life,” he said in the video. Standing in front of Western Pennsylvania's Mon Valley Works steel mill, Fetterman said he and McCormick would work with Trump “to fight and defend the steel way of life right here in the Steel Valley.” Fetterman also praised McCormick despite their partisan differences, saying he was “proud to count him as my great friend.” “How great is John Fetterman?” McCormick said after taking the stage, praising the Democrat for his “friendship” and “courage.” House Speaker Mike Johnson also praised Fetterman's appearance Wednesday, telling Laura Ingraham on Fox News: “John Fetterman is an example of common sense.” But Pennsylvania Republicans who spoke with Newsweek at the convention suggested Fetterman does not need to join their party to win their approval. Guy Ciarrochi, a Chester County Republican delegate from Chester, said Fetterman and McCormick disagree on plenty but have learned “not to be disagreeable.” Asked whether he wanted Fetterman to switch parties, Ciarrochi said no. “For the long-term health of the country, I think it's important that the two parties find a way to work together,” he told Newsweek. Ciarrochi said Fetterman would nevertheless be welcomed in the Republican Party if he chose to join, suggesting there could instead be a “common-sense coalition of old-fashioned Democrats and new Republicans.” Pennsylvania delegate Amber Martin called Fetterman's appearance “spectacular” and “exactly what's needed in our country.” “So, would we like to see Senator Fetterman come to the GOP? Sure,” Martin said. “But I believe that his foundation is old-school Democrat, and I respect that as well.” Joyce Haas, an alternate delegate from Centre County, similarly said she would not push Fetterman to change parties. “I believe he is good for us both ways,” Haas said, whether he is “helping us as a Democrat” or a Republican. Fetterman has developed a close relationship with McCormick while breaking with members of his party on several high-profile issues. He has also shown a willingness to work with Trump since his return to the White House. Fetterman met with Trump at Mar-a-Lago before his inauguration and has since praised the president on issues including steel. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: The Pennsylvania Democrat praised McCormick and vowed to work with Trump as delegates applauded his surprise appearance.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: Colombia's New President Is Following The Trump Playbook On Immigration
news.text: Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella is the latest Latin American leader to mirror the hardline rhetoric of United States President Donald Trump, but experts say his plan to deport thousands of immigrants may not be feasible.Weeks after taking power, de la Espriella announced that his government would begin to carry out operations aimed first at deporting criminals. But later the operation would impact anyone without regular immigration status. "Colombians first, Colombians second, and Colombians third," he said.Unlike Trump, who has dramatically increased deportations from the United States, de la Espriella's party does not hold political control of his country's legislature. Nor, experts say, does the country have the capacity to carry out sweeping immigration raids like those seen in U.S. cities such as Chicago and Los Angeles."In Colombia, I think the rhetoric is going to be easier than the implementation," said Robert Harding, a political science professor at Valdosta State University.De la Espriella's posture reflects his interest in tightly aligning Colombia with the United States. Through his "Shield of the Americas" regional security alliance, Trump has pushed for Latin American countries to impede migration and linked its rise with that of organized crime throughout the region, including illicit gangs like the infamous Venezuela-born Tren de Aragua.For de la Espriella, "it's all a big show — he wants to join this club," said Gimena Sanchez, the Andes director for the human rights advocacy nonprofit Washington Office on Latin America.If realized, the largest impact of de la Espriella's deportation plan would be on the estimated 2.9 million Venezuelans who have migrated to Colombia since 2018 following the country's economic and social collapse. Estimates vary, but it is believed about 850,000 Venezuelans now live in Colombia without regular status, meaning they do not have a visa or residency permit. In 2021, Colombia announced a 10-year temporary protected status for Venezuelans under President Iván Duque, but saw its commitment to regularizing migrants wane under leftwing former President Gustavo Petro.De la Espriella now joins other recently-elected right-wing leaders throughout Latin America in taking a firm stance against immigration, particularly from Venezuela, and linking it to concerns about security.Argentinian President Javier Milei and Chilean President José Antonio Kast, for example, have both sought to appease the United States and their political bases by promising to rein in immigration.But experts noted data indicates the level of deportations from those countries have yet to reach massive levels and might not ever in Colombia, either. Nevertheless, in each case, the rhetoric sends a signal to Washington that immigration is a top concern.In Colombia, immigration wasn't an explicit focal point of de la Espriella's unexpected rise to power in the way it served Trump during his 2024 campaign in the United States.But the Colombian president, who was backed forcefully by Trump in the campaign, sees a clear benefit from a tight alliance with the United States; on the day de la Espriella took office, the U.S. announced it would dedicate a US$1 billion security aid package for Colombia.Diego Chavez-González, a Latin American analyst for the Migration Policy Council, questioned whether an all-out immigration operation would benefit either the United States or Colombia. He warned that sending thousands of immigrants back across the 2,219-kilometer land border between Colombia and Venezuela could make them susceptible to recruitment and exploitation by groups that control the region, such as the National Liberation Army, or ELN."Having irregular status makes them invisible and makes them very vulnerable," Chavez-González said of migrants. "Being harsh on crime is one thing, but I think there is a confusion by many politicians — irregularity is not the cause of crime, irregularity is a consequence of bad policy."The border between Venezuela and Colombia is notoriously porous, with thousands of people crossing every day."If a Venezuelan wants to migrate to Colombia, that person can migrate to Colombia very easily," Chavez-González said.Criminal organizations have a presence not only in rural areas along the border, WOLA's Sanchez noted, further complicating any government efforts to dispel irregular migrants linked to crime."The ones that he's looking for, they're in conflict areas, urban and rural, the country doesn't have control of," Sanchez said.A destabilized border between Colombia and Venezuela has drawbacks for the United States, which is looking to stabilize Latin America firmly under its sphere of influence under the "Donroe Doctrine". But it's also a threat to de la Espriella, whose unexpected ascendency was built on a campaign dedicated to improving security in Colombia.Not only does he face a divided legislature, de la Espriella's administration was also forced to contend with a far more immediate and pressing disaster after an Aug. 10 earthquake left large portions of western Colombia destroyed or damaged.Though he campaigned on reducing the size of the state, de la Espriella was forced to increase his predecessor's budget proposal by about 10% to 634.95 trillion Colombian pesos (approximately $206 billion USD), partly in order to pay for relief in the wake of the earthquake — likely limiting the Colombian government's will to funnel resources into ramped-up immigration enforcement operations.But while enormous raids might not become the norm, the president's rhetoric can have an impact. Immigrant advocacy groups have expressed worry about the spread of misinformation that provokes fear in the immigrant community and have urged migrants not to "self-deport," as they have from countries like the United States.De la Espriella's rhetoric is highly likely to curry favor with Trump, but whether it lands with the Colombian populace remains to be seen, experts said."He's being a typical politician in the sense that he has talked up a big game to a population that is rightfully frustrated, scared and hoping for a miracle," Harding said.
news.summary: If realized, the largest impact of Abelardo de la Espriella's deportation plan would be on the estimated 2.9 million Venezuelans who have migrated to Colombia since 2018 following the country's economic and social collapse.
news.author: Adam Shanks / Latin America Reports

news.title: Fetterman Praises McCormick, Vows To Work With Trump In Pre-Recorded Midterm Convention Video
news.text:
A sitting Democratic senator lent his voice to the Republican Party’s big night, and the political world took notice.

Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman appeared in an unexpected prerecorded video at the GOP’s first-ever midterm convention Wednesday night to introduce Republican Sen. Dave McCormick and pledge cooperation with President Donald Trump on protecting the steel industry, according to Axios. The roughly one-minute message ran during the event in Dallas.

Fetterman used the clip to draw a line between himself and the left flank of his party while affirming he had not left it. (RELATED: Editor Daily Rundown: GOP’s First-Ever Midterm Convention Opens Wednesday In Dallas)

“Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a common-sense Democrat,” Fetterman said in the video. “I’m always going to stand with America. I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and the anti-American way of life.”

SHOCKING MOVE: Democratic Sen. John Fetterman makes a surprise video appearance at the GOP midterm convention, declaring he will reject “the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life.”The appearance is a stunning turn for the first-term senator who skipped his… pic.twitter.com/dnbPPapjh0— Fox News (@FoxNews) September 9, 2026

Standing before Western Pennsylvania’s Mon Valley Works steel mill, Fetterman vowed to join with Trump to defend the steel industry in the region.

McCormick responded warmly to the video as he took the stage. “How great is John Fetterman?” the Republican senator said, praising his colleague for his “friendship” and “courage,” according to CBS News. 

The praise centered on the Nippon Steel investment in U.S. Steel, a deal both Pennsylvania senators came to support, according to NBC News.

Fetterman has drifted from his party for months and now ranks as Trump’s closest Democratic ally in Congress, CNN reported. He skipped his own party’s 2024 convention and has grown deeply unpopular among Democrats. Fetterman and McCormick even started a joint fundraising committee together, an arrangement that drew sharp criticism from the left, according to NBC News.

Fetterman made no announcement about switching parties, though Politico reported in May that Republicans were working hard to woo him. The freshman senator holds an approval rating of almost 80% among Pennsylvania Republicans, but is badly underwater with Democrats and would be highly vulnerable to a 2028 primary challenge.

news.title: Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm polls
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 10 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said that the war with Iran would end immediately after the midterm elections, accusing Tehran of prolonging the conflict in an effort to influence American voters. "I think the war is going to end immediately after the election," Trump told reporters before departing aboard Air Force One for Dallas on Wednesday (local time). Asked why he expected the conflict to end, Trump said: "Because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon." "All they want is a nuclear weapon. And if they had a nuclear weapon, the whole world is in deep trouble," he added. Trump also linked the Iran conflict to the rise in global oil prices, which have climbed above $100 a barrel. "Well, I think it's very easy to explain to America. All you have to do is say, will you let Iran have a nuclear weapon? And the answer is no," he said when asked how he would explain the increase to Americans. The President claimed Iran's economy was in disarray and that its currency had lost its value. "Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump said. "They're going to be tumbling down, and we'll get them down." "I think, for gasoline, we'll get them below $2 a gallon," he added. When asked whether prices would decline before the midterms, Trump said: "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm." Trump said the United States was not currently seeking negotiations with Iran, although he did not rule out the possibility. "Originally, I wanted to make a deal. We're so far down the line. They have very little country left right now, so we're not looking for it," he said. "Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it's not something we're looking at," Trump added. Asked whether he was still seeking a nuclear agreement after Energy Secretary Chris Wright suggested that one might no longer be under consideration, Trump replied: "No." "I'm doing much more than a nuclear deal. There's a lot more than nuclear," he said. "We're going to have nuclear. That's 99.9, but there's going to be a lot of other things on the table that wouldn't have been on the table three months ago." Trump also said US forces had destroyed Iranian vessels during fighting around the Strait of Hormuz. "We've knocked out nine of their ships," he said. "And you're going to see -- you're going to see a lot more. We've taken out about nine of their tankers. Many of them are gonzo." The conflict has entered its seventh month, and renewed fighting around the Strait of Hormuz has pushed benchmark Brent crude above $100 a barrel. The US midterm elections are scheduled for November 3.
news.author: Daklu IANS

news.title: Dem incumbent becomes first sitting governor to lose primary since 2018
news.text: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee lost his Democratic primary Wednesday to businesswoman Helena Foulkes, becoming the first sitting governor in the country since 2018 to be denied his party's nomination. Foulkes, a former CVS executive and current Costco board member, defeated McKee in a rematch of their closely fought 2022 Democratic primary, when McKee edged her by just a few percentage points. McKee's defeat Wednesday adds another incumbent to a growing list of officeholders ousted during the 2026 primary season. McKee first became governor in 2021 after Gov. Gina Raimondo left office to serve as Commerce Secretary in the Biden administration. The former Cumberland mayor and two-term lieutenant governor went on to win his first full term in 2022 after narrowly emerging from a crowded Democratic primary that included Foulkes. INCUMBENT GOP GOVERNOR ROLLS TO PRIMARY VICTORY AFTER KEEPING TRUMP AT A DISTANCE The last sitting governor to lose his party's nomination was Kansas Republican Gov. Jeff Colyer. Colyer lost the 2018 GOP primary to then-Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, backed by Donald Trump at the time, by fewer than 400 votes. Foulkes has spent decades in the private sector, including as a senior executive at Rhode Island-based CVS Health, and later served as CEO of Hudson's Bay Company. She sits on Costco's board of directors. Her 2026 campaign marked Foulkes' second bid for elected office after finishing second to McKee in the 2022 Democratic gubernatorial primary. EX-DEM LOBBYIST FOR COMPANY THAT PROMOTED ADDICTIVE OPIOID CLEARS KEY GUBERNATORIAL HURDLE The rematch centered in part on the candidates' competing arguments over their records and leadership. Foulkes criticized McKee's management of state government, including his administration's handling of the Washington Bridge, which was abruptly closed over structural concerns in December 2023 and remains under reconstruction. McKee defended his administration's record and repeatedly targeted Foulkes' tenure at CVS, suggesting she is an out-of-touch corporate executive and going after her leadership role at the company amid its controversial handling of prescription opioids. news.title: Pakistan delivers Saudi warning to Iran: Rein in the Houthis
news.text: Pakistan has delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in its Yemeni Houthi allies after they stepped up attacks on the kingdom, ​in a coordinated effort to prevent the crisis from spiraling, Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources said. The Houthis struck an airbase in Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities ‌on Tuesday, wounding 73 people, in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Wednesday that Saudi warplanes carried out 54 airstrikes across various Yemeni provinces over the past 12 hours, adding that they would "not go unanswered and unpunished." The escalating conflict, which represents a second theater of war to threaten global energy supplies, comes as Iran and the United States wage their ​biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping in the Gulf region since their war began. Pakistan's warning to Iran carries significant weight because of its defense pact with Saudi Arabia and ​Turkey. While officials in Islamabad stressed any military role would be confined to defending Saudi territory, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said attacks spilling into the ⁠kingdom could trigger a joint security arrangement involving Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad. "An aggression on one country will be considered an aggression on all three countries," Asif said on Pakistani TV. "There is no ambiguity or ​doubt... Unprovoked aggression or spillover... into Saudi Arabia will definitely make this agreement operational." The Pakistani defense ministry, foreign ministry and the military did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Fears of proxy war turning into wider regional crisis Pakistan’s intervention, after years of balancing ties with Saudi Arabia and Iran, has underscored the seriousness of the Houthi attacks. The message to Tehran is clear: rein in the Houthis or risk turning a proxy conflict into a broader regional security crisis, the sources said. A senior regional diplomat said Pakistan had conveyed the message to Iran over the past 24 hours, urging Tehran to use its influence to halt Houthi attacks on Saudi ​Arabia. A senior Iranian official confirmed that Pakistan conveyed the message to Tehran on Tuesday and Tehran's response was that "Iran does not control the Houthis." However, two Iranian sources said Tehran had told the Houthis last ​week to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia. Tehran promised additional funding and weapons, they said, while several Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders had travelled to Yemen to help coordinate the attacks. The regional diplomat said Islamabad was ‌seeking to ⁠restrain the Houthis before the escalation reached a point where Riyadh could press Pakistan to play a more active role in defending it. "Pakistan has an agreement with Saudi Arabia, but I am hopeful the situation will not reach the point where Pakistan has to practically step in," the diplomat told Reuters. "It will pursue a diplomatic solution for now." Pakistani support for Saudis The Pakistani source said Saudi officials had met senior Pakistani and Turkish military representatives in Riyadh to coordinate their response. The three countries agreed that their troops would not enter Yemen and that any response would be launched from Saudi territory, the source added. A ​second Pakistani source said no decision had been ​made to join retaliatory strikes, stressing that ⁠its military pact with Riyadh was defensive and limited to protecting Saudi territory. Pakistani forces could provide military, technical, ground or air support within Saudi Arabia, but would not take part in combat operations on foreign soil, the source said. The pressure campaign waged by Iran and the Houthis could have the ​opposite effect to that intended by Tehran, the regional diplomat said. By targeting Gulf security in a bid to pressure Washington over its blockade of ​Iranian ports, Tehran risks driving ⁠Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and other U.S.-aligned states into closer security coordination rather than fracturing their ties. Trump's blockade of Iran set to continue Regional officials also see little sign that Washington is prepared to relent. President Donald Trump appears committed to maintaining the U.S. blockade until Iran reaches an agreement with Washington, the diplomat said, while Qatar is quietly exploring new proposals aimed at bringing both sides back to negotiations. Another regional source said Saudi ⁠Arabia's military response ​would remain focused on the Houthis rather than Iran itself. Nor do Saudi officials believe Houthi attacks will achieve Tehran's ​broader objective of ending the U.S. blockade. Riyadh is not expected to press Washington to lift the blockade, that source said, stressing that Trump believes sustained economic coercion is the most effective pathway to negotiations. "The question is how much pain Iran can absorb, ​and for how long," the source said. "Trump does not want a military solution. He wants to squeeze them through the blockade."
news.summary: Warning comes after Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia; Pakistan's warning to Iran carries significant weight because of its defense pact with Saudi Arabia and ​Turkey
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Melania Trump's team breaks silence on her husband's devoted 'human printer' aide Natalie Harp
news.text:
Melania Trump's team has finally addressed the president's aide Natalie Harp amid rampant speculation about their close working relationship.

The first lady's top spokesman, Marc Beckman, batted down the wild rumors swirling around Donald Trump and Harp.

'The liberal media is ridiculous,' Beckman told host Stella Escobedo during an interview on Wednesday.

'They don't know anything about the first lady's personal and private life. They don't even take the time to put us on air to cover these incredible achievements that our first lady has accomplished.' 

Harp, 35, was dubbed the 'human printer' for accompanying the president with a portable printer and supplying paper copies of news articles as well as social media posts throughout the day.

'What they need to do is look in the mirror because they’re all attacking this hardworking, very talented, very intelligent person in Natalie Harp,' added Beckman.

'And they're obsessed with the gossip with the first family. And I can tell you firsthand that it’s time for them to become journalists and stop looking at the gossip.'

 Trump and Harp's bond became the center of national media attention in August when Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff told a rally that Trump would rather 'build his ballroom and travel with Natalie' than do his job.

Ossoff was referring to when Harp was among a tiny handful of aides Trump kept beside him as he slipped off Air Force One in Turkey and onto a decoy jet over an Iranian assassination threat. Top cabinet officials, including Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent, were left behind on the larger plane while Harp stayed with the President.

'The media doesn't know about the first lady's private life. Period. The media doesn't know about the first family's life. Period,' said the first lady's advisor. 

'And what they do is they harp on the issues of gossip rather than going ahead and covering the substantial achievements that this first lady and the president also have conducted during this past year and a half.'

Escobedo highlighted Melania's efforts to support children in foster care and those who have aged out of the system.

Aside from her initiatives, the first lady has been seen out in public less than 50 times this year, according to the Daily Beast. 

However, Harp has remained glued to the Trump's side to the point that it raised concerns within the Secret Service and the president's inner circle.

The aide wrote Trump a series of personal letters in 2023, telling him in one: 'You are all that matters to me.'

She also called him her 'Guardian and Protector in this Life,' according to letters reviewed by the New York Times.

Trump told people that same year that Harp was the only person on his team who cared about him: 'All of you will go off and make money ... she'll never leave me.'

It was revealed on Wednesday that the human printer was gifted $45,000, along with two other female aides.

Harp, Chamberlain Harris, 26, and Margo Martin, 31, received $135,000 between them, each identifying Trump as the source of a 'cash gift for the holidays,' according to Politico.

The money came on top of their $150,000 salaries paid by taxpayers, giving each woman a gift worth 30 percent of her annual government pay.

The Daily Mail has contacted the White House, Harp, Harris and Martin.

'The President has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector,' a White House spokesman told Politico.

'The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and, therefore, are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.
news.summary: The first lady's top spokesman downplayed the rumors swirling around Donald Trump and Harp during an interview on Wednesday.
news.author: Editor,Jack Toledo

news.title: Global Merchandise Trade Gains Momentum Despite US Tariffs, Middle East Tensions: WTO
news.text: Geneva, September 09 (QNA) - The global merchandise trade has continued to gain momentum and recover since June, fueled by a surge in demand for the technology sector, The World Trade Organization (WTO) said in its latest report Wednesday.WTO added that this resilience underscores the ability of international merchandise flows to withstand heightened risks stemming from trade protectionism and acute geopolitical disruptions.According to the Goods Trade Barometer -a composite leading indicator released four times a year to provide an early indication of the trajectory of trade two to three months before official statistics are released - the September reading stood at 102.0 points, improving from the previous reading of 101.7 points recorded in June, the report continued. Readings above the 100-point threshold, or baseline, indicate that merchandise trade volumes are growing at a faster pace than their usual rates calculated over recent decades, it added.The Geneva-based organization explained that continued investment and strong global demand for electronic components and semiconductors linked to artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure have served as counterweights, helping offset and mitigate the fallout of the current tensions.Overall, WTO forecast in March that global merchandise trade volume would slow markedly, growing by just 1.9% this year, compared with strong growth of 4.6% in 2025.The organization again warned that the outlook remains clouded by uncertainty, with growth potentially falling to 1.4% under a scenario of persistently high energy prices, particularly amid the ongoing war and military tensions between the United States and Iran, as well as severe disruptions in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global oil supplies pass. In addition, protectionist trade policies are casting a shadow over supply chains following President Donald Trump's imposition of wide-ranging tariffs on major US trading partners.Lastly, WTO stressed that trade growth remains uneven across regions, warning that persistently higher maritime transport costs and shipping rerouting will continue to overwhelm global supply chains through the remainder of the year. (QNA)
news.summary: Geneva, September 09 (QNA) - The global merchandise trade has continued to gain momentum and recover since June, fueled by a surge in demand for the technology sector, The World Trade Organization (WTO) said in its latest report Wednesday.
